The Marble Index and Desertshore both epitomize the idea of the difficult album—a recording so inwardly personal and determinedly anti-commercial that it seemingly reflects the unassailable subconscious of the artist at hand. The defining instrument on The Marble Index is the harmonium played by Nico, which enters on the second track "Lawns of Dawns" like a bad dream. It is a simple, distinctive instrument that relays a rudimentary, folk music aspect to the album that, depending on one's taste, either imparts an ethereal, even spiritual quality to her music or something like a pending migraine or externalized tinnitus.

As the producer, Cale struggled with Nico over this approach, introducing string arrangements and other accompaniments to balance out the droning effects of the harmonium, which, even for him as a sympathetic ear, could prove monotonous by itself.
The result is a bleak and austere album, absent of any guitars or rock music clues, that favors abstract wintry notes over the warmth of human connection.

Desertshore continues in this vein, albeit with some revision. Produced once more with Cale, this time in London and Paris, Nico's third LP is equally stark, though with additional touches like piano on "The Falconer" and "Afraid" that soften the sound and allow for some degrees of warmth, however spectral and momentary.
Lyrically, there is also more expression, with Nico's perspective as a mother surfacing across the tracks.
